# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 14 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus (ch 1-31) / P.Mich. 130 (ch 32+), Shepherd of Hermas 14 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_014_page_001.jpg

---

## Vision 3, Chapter 6

**1** In the middle of the plain she showed me a great white rock, and in the rock a doorway had been hewn that was more brilliant than the sun itself; I marveled at its brightness. **2** Standing around the doorway were twelve virgins: the four stationed at the corners of the doorway seemed more glorious than the rest, though all were glorious. **3** On the outside of the doorway stood two young men, and between them four others of more glorious appearance, clothed in dark garments, with their shoulders bare and their hair unbound, looking somewhat sorrowful. **4** The six builders gave orders to these young men to carry stones for the building. They brought stones from the plain and from a nearby lake. **5** The stones from the plain had already been prepared — hewn and ready — and they were laid into the building as they came, one upon another, so smoothly that their joints could not be seen. **6** The stones from the lake, when placed into the building, became transparent like glass — shining and brilliant — and they adorned the building with their light. **7** I noticed that the aged woman had departed from the scene. After a little while I looked and saw a young woman clothed in bridal dress, with dark slippers and a garland of asphodel. **8** I said to her, "Lady, are you truly in glory? Who are you?" She answered, "I am the Church." I said, "But are you not the aged woman I have seen before?" She replied, "I am the same."

---

### Council Notes

The doorway in the white rock (v. 1) may be the gate of heaven (cf. John 10:9; Rev 4:1). Its exceeding brilliance surpasses the sun — a classic feature of heavenly portals.

The twelve virgins (v. 2) echo the ten virgins of Matthew 25, but here their number corresponds to the twelve gates of the heavenly Jerusalem (Rev 21:12). They guard the entrance to the tower.

The key moment is the Church's self-revelation as the young bride (v. 8): "I am the same." The aging/youth reversal is the Shepherd's central symbol of ecclesial renewal. The Church was seen as old and weary because she was created before all things; she appears young when her members repent and are renewed.

Asphodel at a wedding unites death and new life — the resurrection-community gathered at the threshold.
